name: Fenfluramine/phentermine (fen-phen)

card.summary: A 1990s prescription weight-loss drug pairing withdrawn in 1997 after heart valve damage and pulmonary hypertension were linked to it.
card.note: Fenfluramine and dexfenfluramine were withdrawn from the US market in 1997 over valvular heart disease.

quick.overview:
Fen-phen was the nickname for taking fenfluramine and phentermine together to lose weight. A 1984 trial reported greater weight loss than placebo, and use grew widely in the 1990s.

In 1997 reports of heart valve abnormalities led the FDA to request withdrawal of fenfluramine, and the episode produced tens of thousands of lawsuits.
quick.mechanism: Fenfluramine mainly releases serotonin and phentermine mainly releases norepinephrine, which together suppress appetite. The valve damage is attributed to fenfluramine's activation of 5-HT2B receptors on heart valves.
quick.risks: Documented harms are valvular heart disease and pulmonary hypertension. Fenfluramine and dexfenfluramine are no longer marketed for weight loss in the US.

lead: Fen-phen is the informal name for the combination of the appetite suppressants fenfluramine and phentermine, which was prescribed for weight loss in the United States in the 1990s [1]. People used it to lose body fat, with the appearance goal of a leaner physique and face, through reduced appetite. Fenfluramine mainly releases serotonin, while phentermine mainly releases norepinephrine [1]. Prescribers and patients treated it as a way to lose weight without relying on willpower alone; its marketing in the 1990s leaned on the pitch that exercise was unnecessary [23].

The combination grew popular after a 1984 trial by University of Rochester researchers reported greater weight loss than placebo [1]. In August 1997 a Mayo Clinic report in the New England Journal of Medicine linked it to heart valve abnormalities, and the FDA requested withdrawal of fenfluramine and dexfenfluramine in September 1997 [1]. The episode produced tens of thousands of lawsuits [1].

Fen-phen is no longer on the market. It remains a reference case in discussions of weight-loss drugs, and it is the reason later serotonergic obesity drugs were screened for valve safety [2][7]. Fenfluramine itself returned in a different setting: as Fintepla, a seizure medicine for Dravet and Lennox-Gastaut syndromes, under a restricted distribution programme with echocardiogram monitoring [12][13]. Phentermine alone remained available by prescription, and phentermine now features in combination with topiramate [14].

The story is told in medicine, regulation and law as a case study: Wikipedia and news retrospectives describe the 1984 Rochester trial, heavy marketing, more than six million prescriptions while the drugs were sold, an FDA reviewer who argued for a boxed warning, the 1997 Mayo Clinic valve report, and litigation whose settlements were counted in billions of dollars [1][23][22]. Looksmaxxing forums mention it mostly as history or as a name in lists of banned substances; no discussion of recent use was identified [17][18].

angle.text: Fen-phen was prescribed to reduce appetite so that people lost weight; the cosmetic payoff people sought was a leaner body. It was withdrawn in 1997 after valve disease reports, and is documented here as history.

paras: The combination was prescribed to treat obesity, usually as a long-term regimen. National survey data from the period describe a large rise in prescription of antiobesity medications in the 1990s [3][4]. Fenfluramine was marketed by American Home Products, later Wyeth, as Pondimin, and its dextro-isomer dexfenfluramine as Redux [1].

Outside of obesity treatment, a 1994 report by Hitzig and Rothman suggested that the combination might reduce alcohol and cocaine craving, and rat studies followed; planned NIH human trials were never carried out [1]. A 2002 rat study tested fenfluramine or fluoxetine combined with phentermine on cocaine self-administration [11].

In the mid-1990s the combination was marketed heavily, and a business-press retrospective describes the pitch as weight loss without exercise.[23] A physician-led regimen of the two drugs at the University of Rochester predated the marketing; the same retrospective says it was begun in 1979 and reported in 1992 in 121 patients over four years, though that account does not name the physician.[23]

Fenfluramine alone was introduced in the 1970s and sold modestly because its weight loss was temporary [1]. In the 1984 double-blind University of Rochester trial (Weintraub and colleagues), average weight loss over 24 weeks was 8.4 kg with the combination, 7.5 kg with fenfluramine alone, 10.0 kg with phentermine alone and 4.4 kg with placebo; the authors reported fewer adverse effects with the combination than with either drug alone [1].

The combination was heavily marketed in the 1990s [1]. A later paper examined weight loss together with valvular disease in fen-phen patients [5]. Modern network meta-analyses of obesity drugs compare newer agents; they do not include fen-phen, which left the market decades earlier [15][16].

The August 1997 Mayo Clinic report in the New England Journal of Medicine, by Connolly and colleagues, described 24 people who had taken fen-phen and suggested a link with mitral valve dysfunction; the FDA then received over 100 further reports of valvular heart disease involving the combination or either drug alone [1]. Echocardiograms were abnormal in about 30 percent of people who had taken the combination for up to 24 months, even without symptoms, compared with under 3 percent for use of three months or less [1]. A later study found that the severity of valve disease among affected patients was related to fenfluramine dose [6].

Pharmacology research found that fenfluramine's metabolite stimulates serotonin 5-HT2B receptors on heart valves, producing changes histologically like those of carcinoid disease or ergot-drug exposure [2][7].

The drugs were linked to pulmonary hypertension, a rare and often fatal lung condition. A 1999 review traced the link back to aminorex, an earlier appetite suppressant associated with an epidemic of the disease in Europe [1][8]. In 1994 a Wyeth official reportedly raised concern that fenfluramine's labelling listed four pulmonary hypertension cases when 41 had been observed; no action was taken until 1996 [1].

Pulmonary hypertension was linked to fenfluramine-type drugs alongside valve disease, and the 1994 labelling concern, the death of a 30-year-old patient in February 1997 and the litigation over later-developing cases all concern it.[1][22] Reviews of the aminorex-to-fen-phen history place the episode in a line of anorectic drugs associated with pulmonary hypertension epidemics.[8]

Fenfluramine acts mainly as a serotonin-releasing agent with weaker norepinephrine release, largely through its active metabolite norfenfluramine; it also agonises 5-HT2 receptors [13]. Phentermine is a norepinephrine-releasing agent. Rat studies of phentermine and fenfluramine given separately and as a mixture described their distinct neurochemical effects [9]. Receptorome screening research identified 5-HT2B activation as the likely target responsible for the valve side effects [2][10].

Phentermine acts mainly as a norepinephrine and dopamine releasing agent with weak serotonergic effects, and Wikipedia states the valve problems were attributed to fenfluramine rather than to phentermine.[25] The FDA first approved phentermine in 1959; it is approved for short-term use (up to 12 weeks), is Schedule IV in the US, and was withdrawn from the UK market in 2000.[25] Its adverse effects include fast heart rate, high blood pressure, insomnia and restlessness.[25] The phentermine-topiramate combination Qsymia, developed by Vivus, was rejected by the FDA in 2010 and approved in 2012, after clinicians had been prescribing the pair off-label.[25]

Fenfluramine was developed in the early 1960s, introduced in France in 1963 and approved in the US in 1973; roughly 50 million Europeans were treated between 1963 and 1996 [13]. The term fen-phen dates from the mid-1990s, after the 1984 trial [1].

Fenfluramine alone sold modestly through the 1970s and 1980s because its effect on weight was temporary, according to Wikipedia.[1] Wikipedia reports that in 1994 Wyeth official Fred Wilson raised concerns that fenfluramine's labelling listed four pulmonary hypertension cases when 41 had been observed; no action followed until 1996.[1] Dexfenfluramine was developed by Interneuron Pharmaceuticals, co-founded by Richard Wurtman, which licensed the patent to Wyeth-Ayerst; some neurologists petitioned the FDA to delay approval on the basis of work by George Ricaurte that was later questioned.[24]

Dexfenfluramine (Redux) was introduced in 1995. The FDA medical officer Leo Lutwak pushed for a black box warning, but the drug was approved in 1996 without one, while European regulators required a major warning [1]. A woman of 30 who developed heart problems after a month on fen-phen died in February 1997, and the case was covered by the Boston Herald [1]. After the Mayo report, the FDA asked for withdrawal in September 1997, and fenfluramine was later withdrawn elsewhere; India banned it in 1998 [1][13].
The US regulatory history of appetite suppressants, reviewed in the Annals of Internal Medicine, has swung between approving amphetamine-like drugs and restricting them as risks emerged [4].

After the September 1997 request, the CDC published interim public-health recommendations on valvulopathy in November 1997.[1] On the FDA's part, news coverage in January 2002 reported that Leo Lutwak, the agency's key reviewer, said American Home Products knew of the drugs' problems before withdrawal; the FDA Commissioner declined to answer CBS, and the company said it had acted responsibly and lawfully and denied a 1999 60 Minutes II report that it knew more than it disclosed about pulmonary hypertension.[22] In November 1998 Wyeth-Ayerst published a comparison of heart function in users and non-users that it said showed no significant differences in cardiovascular clinical outcomes.[22]

More than 50,000 product liability lawsuits were filed [1]. An April 2005 American Lawyer article estimated total liability at up to 14 billion US dollars; in February 2005 Wyeth offered settlements of 5,000 to 200,000 dollars to some plaintiffs, and said it had set aside 21.1 billion dollars for lawsuit costs [1].

The Association of Trial Lawyers of America formed a group to pursue American Home Products after the cardiac reports.[1] CBS reported that in October 1999 the company agreed to pay up to 4.83 billion dollars to settle more than 11,000 lawsuits, without admitting wrongdoing; a business retrospective cites about 175,000 claims and a 3.75 billion dollar class-action settlement.[22][23] Sources give differing totals, reflecting different agreements and counting methods.

Fenfluramine and dexfenfluramine were withdrawn from the US market in 1997 [1]. Phentermine alone remained a prescription drug [1]. Fenfluramine is prescription-only in the US and EU as Fintepla for seizures, and it was removed from Schedule IV of the US Controlled Substances Act in December 2022 [13].

Psychiatrist Richard A. Friedman criticised the 'diet doctors' of the period in 1997, arguing that drug trials needed to run well beyond the one year over which fen-phen had been assessed, as summarised in a later retrospective.[23] The Annals of Internal Medicine's history of anorectic regulation and the aminorex-to-fen-phen review describe the episode as the latest in a pattern of anorectic drugs withdrawn for cardiopulmonary harm.[4][8] The 1999 New York Times reporting summarised by Wikipedia faulted Mount Sinai School of Medicine and the CUNY Research Foundation over tests on children, with none reported harmed.[1]

Mentions on T Nation are historical: a 2002 poster recalled that phentermine with fenfluramine and dexfenfluramine formed the combination withdrawn from the market that revived many personal-injury law practices [17]. Other threads list fenfluramine among substances banned in sport and the NFL [18]. No looksmaxxing-forum discussion of fen-phen use was identified.

Preclinical studies in animals have tested fenfluramine plus phentermine and fluoxetine plus phentermine on cocaine self-administration [11]. Fenfluramine has been studied as an antiseizure drug: a 2019 Lancet randomised trial in Dravet syndrome, later trials in Dravet and Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, and a stiripentol-inclusive trial reported on seizure control [12][19][20][21]. Fintepla is approved for Dravet syndrome (US June 2020, EU December 2020) and Lennox-Gastaut syndrome [13].

Wikipedia notes that the 1994 Hitzig and Rothman report of reduced alcohol and cocaine craving is where the term 'fen-phen' is said to originate, and that the NIH human trials designed afterwards were never performed.[1]

The principal human data on the combination are the 1984 Rochester trial, the 1997 Mayo Clinic echocardiographic findings, and later studies of weight loss and valve disease in people who had taken it [1][5][6]. A dose-effect study among patients with valvulopathy found that fenfluramine dose was related to severity [6].

Later fenfluramine trials in epilepsy include a 2019 Lancet randomised, double-blind placebo-controlled trial in Dravet syndrome, a 2020 JAMA Neurology trial in patients on stiripentol-inclusive regimens, a 2022 JAMA Neurology trial in Lennox-Gastaut syndrome and a third phase III Dravet trial reported in 2023 [12][19][20][21].

lore.intro: On T Nation, fen-phen appears as history: a 2002 post recalled the combination as the one withdrawn from the market, and other threads list fenfluramine among substances banned in sport. No looksmaxxing-forum discussion of current use was identified.[17][18]

claims.claim: The two drugs together give more weight loss with fewer side effects than either alone
claims.believers: The 1984 Rochester investigators reported 8.4 kg lost with the combination at 24 weeks versus 4.4 kg for placebo, with fewer adverse effects than either drug alone.[1]
claims.experts: Phentermine alone produced 10.0 kg in the same trial; later reports linked fenfluramine to valve disease and the drug was withdrawn.[1]

claims.believers: Marketing in the 1990s promoted the pair as a way to lose weight without exercise, and prescriptions exceeded six million.[23]
claims.experts: Critics such as Richard Friedman said trials had run too briefly to judge long-term use.[23]

claims.claim: The combination is safe for the heart
claims.believers: Wyeth-Ayerst published a 1998 comparison it said found no significant differences in cardiovascular clinical outcomes.[22]
claims.experts: The 1997 Mayo report described 24 cases, and echocardiograms were abnormal in about 30 percent of people taking the combination for up to 24 months; dose related to severity in a later study.[1][6]

claims.claim: Phentermine alone carries the same valve risk as fen-phen
claims.believers: Because phentermine was half of the pairing, it is sometimes assumed to share fenfluramine's valve risk; phentermine alone stayed on prescription in the US.[25]
claims.experts: Valve disease was attributed to fenfluramine's 5-HT2B activity rather than phentermine, which remained on the US market.[25][2][10]

claims.claim: The company and regulators knew of the risks earlier
claims.believers: FDA reviewer Leo Lutwak said the company knew of problems before 1997.[22]
claims.experts: The company said it acted responsibly and lawfully and denied a 1999 broadcast report that it knew more than it disclosed.[22]

claims.claim: Fen-phen could reduce alcohol and cocaine craving
claims.believers: Hitzig and Rothman suggested this in 1994, and rat studies followed.[1][11]
claims.experts: Planned NIH human trials were never carried out.[1]
